newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.AFRICAN MINISTER SLAMMED FOR RAIN PAYMENT PLAN.
newsitem.headline: S.AFRICAN MINISTER SLAMMED FOR RAIN PAYMENT PLAN.

text.p: Water Affairs and Forestry Minister Kader Asmal has landed up in hot water with South African farmers and foresters for suggesting that they pay for rain.
Given the country's variable rainfall patterns, with many parts being arid, water conservation is generally accepted as being essential.
But farmers believe that Asmal is taking things too far when he says that water is a national asset which must be paid for -- and that includes rain.
Although Asmal has not spelled out details of such a measure, he recently indicated that this was one of the issues he will be looking at in the country's new water management programme.

According to Effective Farming magazine, Asmal is particularly targeting the forestry industry despite the fact that one of his special advisers had admitted that well managed timber plantations gave one of the best returns on the water available for commercial exploitation.

"He (the adviser) went on to say that afforestation is a very significant source of employment and foreign exchange and compares very favourably with many competing land-use options," the magazine said.
In addition, the environmental damage caused by afforestation was far lower than that caused by unemployment and poverty.
The magazine said Asmal's views were probably based on the historical view that forestry was a "water guzzler" which used an inordinate amount of water to produce a cubic metre of saleable product.

However, it said, Water Affairs Department chief scientist Ciek van der Zyl concluded in 1996 that at most two percent of rainfall runoff in the country was used for timber with the other sectors in agriculture probably using 70 percent.

"Van der Zyl said that timber plantations were perhaps the most efficient users of water of all dryland crops. Yet his minister has no proposals to introduce permits for maize or wheat, ground nuts or pasture grass," the magazine said.
Forestry is the only agricultural sector in which permits are needed to plant anything. The magazine said this was "seriously delaying" further development in the industry.
